content: Personnel at the healthcare facility were able to palpate fetal parts during a vaginal examination. The individual accompanying the patient to the facility could only report that she had been experiencing pains for more than a day and a half. The underlying cause of the condition was classified as Group 5, which includes other obstetric complications. The specific category was identified as obstructed labor, not otherwise specified (NOS). No additional contributing conditions were detailed. This classification will help identify: The number of deaths resulting from obstructed labor. The number of women who die from treatable conditions, such as those requiring blood transfusions or antibiotics. This information will guide programs to address gaps in care during the antenatal and intrapartum periods. The WHO's application of ICD-10 to deaths during pregnancy, childbirth, and the puerperium (ICD-MM) provides appropriate B codes to describe deaths where HIV or AIDS is the underlying cause, even when pregnancy is incidental. This approach reduces confusion and standardizes statistical reporting. Anemia: Except in cases of pre-existing conditions like sickle cell disease or thalassemia, anemia is often secondary to infections, malnutrition, or bleeding. Anemia rarely causes death on its own. In this guide, anemia is considered a contributing factor to maternal death. Even when anemia complicates postpartum hemorrhage, it is almost always the hemorrhage itself that directly causes death. Tetanus: Obstetric tetanus (ICD-10 code A34) is a rare cause of maternal death. For classification purposes, in the absence of detailed clinical information about the infection's course, it is considered a direct maternal cause of death under the group pregnancy-related infection. If tetanus exposure and infection result from an obstetric event, such as abortion or puerperal sepsis, the death is classified under the respective direct cause of death. Malnutrition: While not a direct cause of death, malnutrition may contribute to maternal mortality. Female Genital Mutilation (FGM): FGM is prevalent in some regions and can contribute to maternal death due to scarring, which may lead to prolonged labor, uterine atony, puerperal sepsis, or severe lower genital tract trauma from tearing of scar tissue. HIV and AIDS: There is a tendency to attribute all deaths in individuals with HIV or AIDS to AIDS itself. However, women with HIV may die from AIDS or with HIV. It is important to distinguish maternal deaths in HIV-infected women that are directly related to pregnancy complications, such as incomplete abortion complicated by hemorrhage or tetanus, or ectopic pregnancy. These are considered direct maternal deaths. In such cases, HIV or AIDS may coexist but is not the underlying cause of death. Conversely, AIDS-related indirect maternal deaths occur when pregnancy exacerbates HIV, making it the underlying cause of death. These deaths are categorized under Group 7 (non-obstetric complications). Proper reporting of the interaction between HIV/AIDS and pregnancy will guide coders. Rarely, an HIV-positive woman may die of a fatal HIV complication while pregnant, such as HIV wasting syndrome. In these cases, the pregnancy is incidental, and HIV/AIDS is the underlying cause of death, coded under ICD-10 block B20-B24. These are termed HIV-related deaths during pregnancy, delivery, or puerperium and are not considered maternal deaths. Classifying cases by HIV status provides a clearer understanding of the role of HIV/AIDS in maternal mortality. Obesity, Depression, and Domestic Violence: Obesity is an increasing concern, and collecting data on its impact on maternal deaths can improve understanding. Similarly, depression and domestic violence are contributory conditions, but gathering information on every case may be challenging. Suicide: The ICD-10 and ICD-MM recommend collecting all relevant information about events leading to death. Maternal deaths due to suicide, coded under Chapter XX in vital registration data, are not included in international maternal mortality estimates under current methodology. However, when included in surveillance reporting, they are part of maternal mortality estimation datasets. Antenatal and postpartum suicides are grouped under direct causes of death in the Other category. This classification is recommended even if a definitive diagnosis of puerperal psychosis or postpartum depression cannot be established. The WHO's application of ICD-10 to deaths during pregnancy, childbirth, and the puerperium (ICD-MM) builds upon the ICD-10 framework to provide a useful tool for program officers, healthcare workers certifying deaths, statistical offices, and researchers. It aims to improve the quality of data on maternal deaths, enhance data comparability, and inform program development to reduce maternal mortality. The guide's simplicity and alignment with ICD concepts make it accessible to end users. Future research on its application is necessary to refine its use. Achieving Millennium Development Goal 5 (MDG 5) requires understanding both the magnitude and causes of maternal deaths. Currently, only about one-third of WHO Member States provide high-quality vital registration data, and misclassification of pregnancy-related deaths remains an issue. The guide, along with a pregnancy checkbox on death certificates, aims to improve data accuracy and attribution. For countries with some capacity to capture vital registration events, the guide can enhance data quality. In settings relying on special surveys, the ICD-MM improves data comparability.
